name: Hydrogen-sponge shield wall
subtitle: a spacecraft wall that shields and fuels

effects.effect: sponge-like crystals with a huge inner surface trap one chosen gas
radiation from space grows stronger with altitude

effect: sponge-like crystals with a huge inner surface trap one chosen gas
how: On a Mars voyage the crew would take a career's worth of radiation, and the best shield per kilogram is hydrogen, which splits the incoming particles into harmless fragments rather than making new ones. Liquid hydrogen boils away over a two-year trip, so the wall is packed instead with sponge-like crystals that hold hydrogen in their pores at modest pressure and give it back when heated; boron mixed in mops up the stray neutrons the shield itself creates. The same wall is the ship's fuel tank.
obstacle: Today's best sponges hold only a few percent of their own weight in hydrogen at room temperature, which is not yet enough wall for the mass.
why: One mass does two jobs: the best light shield is also the fuel you brought.
real: NASA screened 64 hydrogen-storing MOFs and metal hydrides as radiation shielding (10% beat HDPE in solar-particle simulations) and a 2025 EPJ Plus study extended this to galactic cosmic rays, with ESA flagging MOF powder handling as the barrier, but all of it is simulation and no shielding wall has been built or flown.
